How we came to blame ourselves The shift toward private blame was gradual. In 1859 Samuel Smiles pub- lished Self-Help, a bestseller preaching that character, not circumstance, decides a person's lot. It suited an industrial age eager to reward striving and to explain poverty as a shortage of it. The idea travelled well and never left. Today it speaks through motivational posters and career advice, promising that every set- back is a lesson waiting for the right at- titude. It flatters the fortunate and quietly indicts everyone else. what they should have done differently.
What the missing planes could tell us During the Second World War, the mathematician Abraham Wald was asked to help decide where to add ar- mour to returning bombers. The military had mapped the bullet holes on the planes that made it home and proposed reinforcing those areas. Wald saw the flaw. The planes that mattered were the ones that never came back and their damage was invisible. The armour be- longed where the survivors were un- harmed. Failure works the same way. We study winners, extract their habits and call the result a method. The many who followed identical habits and vanished do not give interviews. The story of suc- cess is written by survivors, which makes luck look like skill and ordinary misfortune look like a personal defect.

A study led by Drahota, Costall and Reddy found that listeners could distin- guish between different kinds of smile, not just smiling from not smiling. The voice, it seems, keeps a record of how a smile was made and whether it was spontaneous or arranged for the occa- sion. Anyone who has endured a customer service script knows the difference. A smile applied like a coat of paint sounds like exactly that. Ears that quietly copy Hearing a smile is one thing. What happens inside us when we do is another. A team in Paris led by Pablo Arias, Pascal Belin and Jean-Julien Aucoutu- rier digitally altered recordings of ordi- nary speech so that the voices sounded as though their owners were smiling. They then recorded the electrical activ- ity in the facial muscles of people listen- ing. The zygomaticus major, the muscle that pulls the corner of the mouth up- ward, stirred in response. The research- ers reported that this happened even when listeners were not consciously aware of what had changed in the voice. In other words, the listener's face began to answer before the listener knew there was a question. This fits a long-running idea in psy- chology that expression and feeling travel in both directions. new stage. When Alexander Graham Bell's invention spread in the late nine- teenth century, it removed the face from conversation for the first time at scale. Telephone companies, sensing the risk, went so far as to coach their operators. The phrase "the voice with a smile" be- came a well-worn slogan of the industry, a promise that warmth could survive the wire. It was commercial advice, but it was also good psychology. Deprived of a face, listeners did not stop searching for one. They turned to the voice and read it more carefully. We saw the same instinct again in re- cent years, when masks hid the lower half of millions of faces. People spoke of missing smiles and many noticed that they had begun to listen differently. Some found themselves reading the eyes more closely. Others became attuned to the small brightening in a shop assis- tant's greeting, a change that had always been there but had gone unnoticed while the mouth was visible. Our senses, it turns out, are less like separate windows than like members of a committee. When one is silenced, the others speak up.
